description: The bacterial organism studied as the subject of the paper. It serves as the experimental model whose chemotactic behavior and information acquisition are analyzed in relation to gradient climbing performance.

The directed movement behavior by which Escherichia coli navigates chemical gradients. In this study it is the focal biological process whose performance is constrained by information acquisition and signaling.
The environmental gradient of chemical concentration that E. coli senses and climbs during chemotaxis. It represents the directional stimulus driving the behavioral response.

The informational quantity used in the paper to characterize how much environmental signal is available to the organism and how it constrains behavioral performance. It is central to the theoretical limit on gradient-climbing speed.

entity_name: THEORETICAL LIMIT ON THE SPEED WITH WHICH CELLS CLIMB GRADIENTS
description: A derived theoretical bound relating information acquisition rate to the maximum achievable gradient-climbing speed. It functions as the analytical framework used to assess whether observed chemotactic performance approaches an information-based limit.
The measured behavioral performance endpoint describing how quickly cells move up chemical gradients. It is the observed outcome compared against the theoretical information-based bound.
The quantified rate at which cells obtain information through their chemotaxis signaling pathway. It is used to relate sensory input to behavioral performance and to derive the theoretical limit.

The sensory-motor signaling pathway in E. coli that acquires and transmits information from the environment to behavior. It mediates the conversion of chemical-gradient information into movement decisions.

The decision-making process by which E. coli determines whether it is swimming up-gradient. The paper emphasizes that these decisions are made with limited information and are partly decoupled from useful gradient-climbing information.

The informational threshold referenced as the amount required to determine whether cells are swimming up-gradient. It serves as a benchmark for evaluating how much information is actually used in behavioral decisions.

The transmission step by which information from the chemotaxis signaling pathway is converted into observable behavior. The paper notes that some information is lost during this communication process.
Integrated pathways linking sensory information acquisition to motor output. The paper suggests these pathways may have evolved to use environmental information efficiently.

The bacterial population studied as the experimental subject in the chemotaxis experiments. It is the organism whose collective movement and response to attractant dynamics are measured under varying stimulus frequencies.

The population-level bacterial subject whose synchronized oscillatory response and phase behavior are analyzed in relation to attractant waveform frequency. It represents the collective behavioral unit in the microfluidic experiments.

The directed movement response of Escherichia coli to chemical attractants. In this study it is characterized as frequency-dependent, with distinct population responses at low versus fast-changing attractant frequencies.

Spatially and temporally varying chemical attractant inputs used to stimulate E. coli chemotaxis. The scenario includes changing source dynamics and stimulus frequency, which shape the observed population response.

The experimental environment in which the chemotaxis measurements were performed. It provides controlled spatial and temporal variation of attractant sources for observing bacterial population behavior.
The observed chemotactic response pattern that changes with stimulus frequency. It includes synchronized oscillation at low frequency and reduced, out-of-phase response in fast-changing environments.
The measured collective behavioral outcome of the E. coli population in response to attractant waveform changes. It is described by response magnitude and phase relative to the attractant.
The temporal pattern of the attractant stimulus applied to the bacterial population. Its frequency determines whether the population response is synchronized or out of phase.
A well-known continuum chemotaxis model used as a reference framework for interpreting bacterial movement. The observed frequency-dependent behavior is reported to be inconsistent with this equation.

A proposed analytical framework intended to describe population-level E. coli chemotaxis behavior. It incorporates pathway dynamics, finite adaptation time, and attractant consumption rate to explain the experiments.
The internal signaling and response dynamics underlying the population-level chemotaxis behavior. These dynamics form the mechanistic basis of the proposed continuum model.
A temporal biological property describing delayed adaptation of the chemotactic response. It is included in the model to account for frequency-dependent behavior.
The rate at which the bacterial population consumes attractant, affecting local stimulus dynamics and contributing to the observed response patterns.
The range of temporal frequencies used to vary the attractant stimulus in the microfluidic experiments. Different frequencies produce distinct chemotactic response regimes.
The bacterial subject/population studied in the paper. It is the organism in which c-di-GMP-dependent chemotaxis regulation, flagellar motor behavior, and swimming performance are examined.

A ubiquitous bacterial second messenger that serves as a central regulatory molecular signal. In this study it is the key regulatory feature whose elevated levels alter chemotaxis-related motor behavior in E. coli.
An effector protein of c-di-GMP in E. coli. When bound to c-di-GMP, it interacts with the flagellar motor and mediates changes in motor speed and clockwise bias.
The bacterial motility apparatus targeted by the c-di-GMP::YcgR complex and by chemotaxis signaling inputs. It is the functional site where motor speed and clockwise rotation bias are modulated.

The phosphorylated chemotaxis response regulator that participates upstream in the chemotaxis pathway and interacts with the flagellar motor. The study reports that its binding to the motor is noncompetitive with c-di-GMP::YcgR.
The signaling pathway governing bacterial chemotactic responses. In this paper, elevated c-di-GMP levels are shown not to affect the upstream portion of this pathway down to CheY-P concentration.
The biological process of directed bacterial movement in response to chemical gradients. It is the main functional process assessed for sensitivity to elevated c-di-GMP levels in E. coli.
The observed behavioral output of the chemotaxis system measured in E. coli cells. These responses were assayed to determine whether elevated c-di-GMP levels altered chemotaxis performance.

A quantitative motility outcome representing net chemotactic movement. The study uses stochastic simulations to show that opposing effects on motor speed and clockwise bias largely cancel in this endpoint.
The rotational speed of the flagellar motor, treated as a functional motility endpoint. Elevated c-di-GMP levels reduce this parameter, influencing swimming behavior and chemotactic performance.

Clockwise rotation bias of the flagellar motor, a motility-related endpoint. Elevated c-di-GMP levels decrease CW bias, contributing to altered swimming behavior while preserving near-intact chemotaxis.
A fluorescence-based measurement approach used to assess molecular interactions in the study. It was used to test whether there is competitive binding between CheY-P and c-di-GMP::YcgR at the motor.

A fluorescence resonance energy transfer assay used to measure chemotactic responses in E. coli cells. It provided experimental evidence that elevated c-di-GMP levels do not affect the upstream chemotaxis pathway down to CheY-P concentration.

A computational modeling framework used to evaluate how changes in motor speed and CW bias affect chemotactic drift velocity. It supports the conclusion that these effects compensate each other under elevated c-di-GMP conditions.

The experimental condition of increased intracellular c-di-GMP signaling. It is the central perturbation examined for its effects on chemotaxis, motor behavior, and the transition from motile to sedentary bacterial life.

A motile bacterial pathogen subgroup characterized by flagella and active movement, highlighted for using chemotaxis to control localization in host tissues.
Directed movement process used by bacterial pathogens to navigate host environments in response to nutrients, toxins, and molecular cues; central mechanism in localization and disease progression.
Movement-related biological process that chemotaxis directs in pathogens, enabling spatial localization within the host.
External nutrient cues sensed by pathogens in the host environment that guide chemotactic behavior and support survival.
Host- or environment-associated harmful chemical cues sensed by pathogens that influence chemotactic navigation and localization.
General chemical signals in the host environment that are detected by bacterial pathogens and used to direct chemotaxis.
The internal biological environment in which bacterial pathogens localize, sense cues, colonize tissues, and cause disease.
Host tissue locations characterized by inflammation or injury that attract pathogen colonization and are emphasized as key disease-relevant niches.
Nutrients obtained from the host, especially from damaged tissue, that provide fitness advantages to pathogens during colonization.
Injured host tissue that serves as a nutrient source and colonization niche for pathogens exhibiting injury tropism.
Preference of pathogens for injured tissue sites, contributing to localization at damage sites and potentially worsening disease outcomes.
Persistent inflammatory state proposed as a downstream pathological consequence of pathogen injury tropism and colonization.
Disease endpoint described as a possible downstream consequence of chronic inflammation promoted by pathogen injury tropism.
The bacterial sensing and signaling systems that enable chemotaxis and are proposed as therapeutic targets for inhibiting pathogen localization and disease.
Therapeutic agents used against bacterial infection that may act synergistically with chemotaxis inhibition for more effective eradication.
The process by which pathogens establish themselves at specific host sites, driven by chemotaxis and linked to inflammation and injury niches.
Overall disease-relevant patient outcomes that may be worsened by pathogen injury tropism and subsequent inflammatory consequences.

Chemical attractant substances that bacteria move toward during chemotaxis. In the text, nutrients function as the positive directional cue that drives bacterial localization and motion.

Experimental or observational setup containing nutrient sources used in early studies of bacterial localization. This setting provided a chemical gradient or attractant context for observing chemotactic behavior.
A navigation process in which animals use chemical cues to orient movement. It is cited as a broader biological-scale example of chemotaxis-like behavior.
Developmental movement of cells within an organism. The abstract uses this as another cross-scale example of chemotactic or chemotaxis-related directional movement.
Historical period in which early observations of bacterial chemotaxis were made. It provides temporal context for the development of the field rather than a biological exposure setting.

A bacterial signal-transduction process that controls movement direction by regulating flagellar rotation. It is the central biological process discussed in the abstract and is used as a model system for understanding excitation and adaptation mechanisms.

The rotational movement of the bacterial flagellar motor that determines swimming direction. It is the immediate functional output regulated during chemotaxis.

A key chemotaxis response regulator protein that is activated by phosphorylation and controls flagellar motor switching. It interacts with CheA, the motor switch, and CheZ to regulate excitation and adaptation.

A kinase that can autophosphorylate and mediates phosphorylation of CheY. Its activity is controlled by chemoreceptors and it functions upstream in the chemotaxis signaling cascade.
Receptor proteins that control CheA activity in response to stimuli. They provide the sensory input that regulates the chemotaxis phosphorylation cascade.

The default direction of flagellar rotation before CheY-mediated switching. It serves as the baseline rotational state in the chemotaxis response.
The activated phosphorylated form of CheY that dissociates from CheA, binds the motor switch, and interacts with CheZ. It is the active signaling species in chemotaxis control.
A phosphatase that binds phosphorylated CheY and modulates its oligomeric state and dephosphorylating activity. It contributes to termination/adaptation in chemotaxis signaling.
The multimeric assembly state of CheZ that is altered by phosphorylated CheY binding. This structural state is linked to phosphatase activity regulation.
The enzymatic activity of CheZ that removes phosphate from phosphorylated CheY. It is modulated through changes in CheZ oligomeric state.
The initial chemotactic response phase controlled by CheY phosphorylation. It is one of the two major response mechanisms discussed.
The response-resetting phase of bacterial chemotaxis that allows cells to adjust to persistent stimuli. CheY phosphorylation and CheZ-mediated dephosphorylation are implicated in this process.

entity_name: LATERAL CONTROL AT THE RECEPTOR LEVEL

A proposed regulatory mechanism in which metabolites link central metabolism with chemotaxis. It represents a potential modulatory input to the chemotaxis network.
The core metabolic network that may be linked to chemotaxis through metabolite-mediated control. It is referenced as a source of regulatory coupling.

The microbial subjects discussed in the review as the organisms performing chemotaxis. They are the primary biological population whose migratory behavior, nutrient uptake, and ecological roles are being analyzed across laboratory and environmental settings.

The directed movement behavior of bacteria in response to chemical gradients. In this text it is the central biological process whose ecological roles are examined, including foraging, colony expansion, host or partner localization, and spatial segregation.

An ecological behavioral process in which bacteria use chemotaxis to enhance acquisition of nutrients and energy. It represents the traditional functional interpretation of bacterial chemotaxis in the abstract.
The resource acquisition process that bacterial chemotaxis is said to enhance. It is a functional outcome of chemotactic movement and is central to bacterial growth and survival.

Chemical compounds that attract bacteria and guide chemotactic movement. The text notes that some less nutritious compounds can act as strong chemoattractants, highlighting their ecological and behavioral significance.

entity_name: LOCALIZATION OF HOSTS OR SYMBIOTIC PARTNERS

The process by which bacterial communities become spatially separated, contributing to microbial diversity. The abstract identifies this as a consequence of chemotaxis in communities.
The broad range of natural environments in which bacterial chemotaxis has been observed. This setting category includes diverse ecological contexts beyond laboratory systems.
Experimental research settings in which most current insights into bacterial chemotaxis have been obtained. These studies typically use model organisms under controlled conditions.
Organisms used as experimental models to study bacterial chemotaxis. The abstract notes that much of the current understanding is based on these laboratory models.

A tracking approach proposed for systematically mapping when and where bacteria are motile across generations. It is described as a method for studying bacterial movement in dynamic environments.
Changing environmental contexts in which bacterial motility and chemotaxis are proposed to be mapped. These settings are important for understanding behavior over time and across conditions.

Field-based observational or measurement approaches used to study bacterial motility and chemotaxis in their native environments. The abstract highlights these approaches as important for understanding ecological roles.
A host-associated environmental setting mentioned as part of the range of in situ contexts for studying bacterial motility and chemotaxis.
A natural environmental setting mentioned as part of the range of in situ contexts for studying bacterial motility and chemotaxis.
The biochemical process of energy and nutrient utilization that the abstract identifies as interacting with growth in the context of bacterial motility and chemotaxis.
The broader microbial biological context in which chemotaxis contributes to ecological function and survival. It represents the overarching population-level domain discussed in the review.

The microbial population whose movement behavior is being described and regulated by chemotaxis. It serves as the broader biological subject for the processes and applications discussed.

A spatial variation in chemical concentration that acts as the environmental cue guiding bacterial movement. In this context it represents the directional stimulus sensed during chemotaxis, including beneficial and toxic gradients.

Surface appendages responsible for bacterial motility. Their rotation enables run-and-tumble behavior and is a key structural component of chemotactic movement.

The intracellular protein network that regulates bacterial chemotaxis by processing sensory signals and transmitting them to the flagellar motor. It represents the signaling architecture underlying chemotactic control.
Intracellular proteins that process sensory signals and relay them to the flagellar motor. They function as downstream components of the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
A community-assembly process in which bacteria attach and develop structured biofilms. The text identifies bacterial chemotaxis as an important contributor to this process.
A bacterial communication process that coordinates group behavior based on population density. It is listed as a biological process influenced by bacterial chemotaxis.
Disease-causing capability of bacteria, including mechanisms that promote infection and virulence. The review states that bacterial chemotaxis plays an important role in this outcome.
Infection of a host organism by bacteria. It is described as a biological outcome in which bacterial chemotaxis has an important functional role.
An applied environmental process in which bacteria are used to degrade or remove contaminants. The text notes bacterial chemotaxis as a potential enabling feature for this application.
The transfer of genetic material between organisms outside of vertical inheritance. The review mentions bacterial chemotaxis as potentially useful in this process or application context.
An applied delivery application in which bacterial chemotaxis may be exploited for targeted transport. It is mentioned as a future industrial or biomedical application of chemotaxis.

An experimental platform used to study bacterial behavior under carefully controlled microenvironments with high spatial and temporal resolution. In this text it functions as the enabling method for observing chemotaxis and generating controlled gradients.

The motile sensing-and-response process by which bacteria detect and move along chemical gradients. It is the central biological process discussed, with relevance to pathogenesis, biofilm formation, bioremediation, and ocean carbon cycling.
Cell movement behavior studied using microfluidics, providing the broader biological context for chemotaxis observations. It is characterized by dynamic responses in controlled microenvironments.

Carefully controlled experimental environments created to study cell behavior, especially gradient sensing and chemotaxis. They provide the physical context in which microfluidic observations are made.
Bacterial cells studied in a motile, non-surface-adherent state. They are the primary subject population for microfluidic chemotaxis experiments described in the abstract.

Cells attached to a surface, used as a contrasting experimental subject population in chemotaxis studies. The text notes that their experimental challenges differ from those of free-swimming bacteria.
Engineered microfluidic devices developed to generate flow-free, steady gradients of arbitrary shape. They are key tools enabling modern chemotaxis experiments.

Microfluidic devices or device classes designed to produce controlled chemical gradients for chemotaxis studies. The latest generation is highlighted as especially useful for biological and ecological applications.

A bacterial decision-making process in which cells distinguish among competing gradient cues. It is identified as a mechanistic question addressed by recent microfluidic studies.
A disease-relevant outcome influenced by bacterial chemotaxis, reflecting its role in infection and host interaction. The text lists it among major processes affected by chemotactic behavior.
A microbial community outcome associated with bacterial chemotaxis. It is cited as one of the important processes in which chemotaxis plays a fundamental role.

An environmental application/outcome linked to bacterial chemotaxis, where directed movement can influence pollutant degradation or environmental cleanup. It is mentioned as a process affected by chemotactic behavior.

The marine environmental setting in which large-scale consequences of bacterial chemotaxis are considered. It provides the ecological context for modeling chemotaxis in realistic environments.

The scientific research setting in which bacterial chemotaxis is used as a model system to understand sensing and response to gradients. It frames the methodological and conceptual motivation for the work.

A scientific user population seeking to unravel the fundamental mechanisms of bacterial chemotaxis. They are highlighted as primary beneficiaries of the latest microfluidic gradient generators.

The chemotaxis signaling pathway in Escherichia coli used as an ideal model for understanding bacterial sensing and directional movement. It encompasses receptor-mediated signal recognition, adaptation, amplification, and output control.
Cellular signaling pathways used by bacteria to detect environmental changes and guide movement. In this text, they provide the mechanistic framework for sensing and responding to chemoeffectors.
The changing external conditions sensed by bacteria through chemotaxis pathways. This environmental context triggers signaling responses that alter taxis behavior.

Mechanistic processes by which chemoreceptor signals are converted into downstream on-off output states. These mechanisms underlie chemotaxis sensitivity, adaptation, and amplification.
The binary signaling output state produced by chemotaxis receptor systems. It reflects the functional readout of signal transduction and controls downstream taxis responses.
A functional performance characteristic of the chemotaxis system indicating strong responsiveness to small changes in chemoeffector concentration or environmental cues.
The adaptive process by which bacterial chemotaxis signaling adjusts to persistent stimuli while maintaining responsiveness. It is a key property of the receptor signaling network.

The ability of the chemotaxis system to respond across a broad range of stimulus intensities. It is a functional output of receptor organization and signaling architecture.

Well-controlled spatial gradients of chemical concentration applied to the bacterial system. These gradients constitute the experimental stimulus/exposure scenario that drives chemotactic behavior and enables analysis of sensing rules.

The concentration of ligand forming the chemical stimulus, including its spatial gradient and average level near the peak response region. It is the key environmental variable governing the chemotactic response.

External chemical or environmental signals detected by motile bacteria that initiate chemotactic responses. These cues drive movement toward more favorable locations through signal transduction.

The directed movement process by which bacteria respond to environmental cues. It is the central biological system described, integrating sensing, signal transduction, and motility control.

Conserved prokaryotic signaling pathways that mediate responses to environmental cues in chemotaxis. They convert external chemical information into intracellular phosphorylation changes and behavioral output.

The intracellular interpretation and integration of chemotactic signals within receptor assemblies. It shapes phosphorylation responses and ultimately bacterial movement decisions.

A chemotaxis receptor implicated in the competition that governs escape band formation. It is part of the molecular sensing machinery controlling bacterial directional response.
A chemotaxis receptor implicated in the competition that governs escape band formation. It is a key molecular feature in the signaling network underlying bacterial movement decisions.

An adaptor protein that participates in chemoreceptor array formation. It helps organize chemoreceptors with CheA into large hexagonal signaling arrays, contributing to chemotaxis control.
A kinase component of the bacterial chemotaxis signaling complex. Together with chemoreceptors and CheW, it forms large hexagonal arrays that mediate directional movement responses.
Receptor proteins embedded in the inner membrane that can serve as scaffolds for chemoreceptor arrays. Their membrane localization determines one major spatial organization mode for the arrays.
Cytoplasmic receptor proteins that can form chemoreceptor arrays without membrane embedding. They represent an alternative receptor class contributing to intracellular array localization.

Higher-order supramolecular assemblies formed by chemoreceptors, CheW, and CheA. These arrays are the functional signaling structures underlying bacterial chemotactic directionality and can be membrane-associated or cytoplasmic.
The bacterial membrane compartment where transmembrane receptor-based chemoreceptor arrays can be embedded. It provides a spatial context for array localization and signaling organization.
The intracellular compartment where soluble receptor-based chemoreceptor arrays can form. It is an alternative localization setting for chemotaxis signaling assemblies.

The spatial organization process governing where chemoreceptor arrays localize within bacterial cells. This pattern is linked to array segregation during division and to the production of chemotactically competent progeny.

entity_name: SEGREGATION OF ARRAYS BETWEEN DAUGHTER CELLS
description: The partitioning process that distributes chemoreceptor arrays to daughter cells during cell division. It is important for inheritance of chemotactic capability and is driven by multiple evolved mechanisms.
The bacterial reproductive process during which chemoreceptor arrays must be segregated to daughter cells. It provides the biological context for inheritance of chemotactic competence.
The functional offspring outcome resulting from proper segregation of chemoreceptor arrays. These progeny retain the ability to perform chemotaxis effectively.
A mechanism that can drive segregation or positioning of chemoreceptor arrays through spontaneous assembly behavior. It is one of the evolved mechanisms mentioned for array distribution.
Spatial cues or structural features within the cell that help guide chemoreceptor array positioning and segregation. They function as positional determinants in bacterial organization.
Proteins related to ParA that are utilized as part of mechanisms driving chemoreceptor array segregation. They contribute to spatial inheritance of arrays during cell division.
The directed movement process by which bacteria move toward favorable conditions. It is controlled by chemoreceptors and their associated signaling arrays and is central to the paper's topic.
The favorable growth outcome that bacteria achieve by adapting to their environment and moving toward beneficial conditions. It is the broader physiological endpoint motivating chemotactic behavior.
Environmental conditions toward which bacteria move during chemotaxis. They represent the external context that directional movement seeks to reach.

The bacterial population discussed as the biological subject of the chemotaxis system. These organisms actively move and regulate directional behavior through conserved signaling pathways, making them the primary experimental and conceptual population in the text.

A single bacterial cellular context in which chemotaxis signaling occurs. It serves as the organizational unit containing chemoreceptors and signaling proteins that collectively generate the chemotactic response.

The directed movement response regulated by bacteria in response to stimuli. In this text, it is described as a highly conserved chemosensory signal-transduction process governed by networked protein interactions and system-wide regulation.

The conserved signaling machinery that mediates bacterial chemotaxis. It integrates sensory input and transduces it into behavioral responses, forming the mechanistic basis of the system discussed in the abstract.

The protein components involved in bacterial chemotaxis signaling and regulation. They are the molecular entities analyzed through biochemical parameters, protein structures, and interaction maps, and they form the network underlying the response.
The signaling and regulatory proteins that participate in chemotaxis. The text emphasizes that thousands of these proteins form a highly interconnected network through protein-protein interactions.

A functional subset of chemotaxis proteins responsible for transmitting signals and regulating the chemotactic response. They are described as numerous and networked, contributing to system robustness and responsiveness.

Sensory receptor proteins that detect multiple stimuli and initiate chemotaxis signaling. The text notes that different chemoreceptors have distinct sensory modalities and interact to shape cooperativity and sensitivity.

The interaction process by which chemotaxis proteins connect into a highly interconnected signaling network. These interactions are central to system-wide analyses, network architecture, and the emergent properties of the chemotaxis response.
A system-level property of the chemotaxis response influenced by interactions among chemoreceptors. It reflects how combined receptor behavior affects signaling output and sensitivity.
The responsiveness of the chemotaxis system to stimuli. It is modulated by receptor interactions and contributes to how effectively bacteria detect and respond to environmental cues.

The ability of the chemotaxis system to maintain function despite perturbations in biochemical parameters. The text identifies robustness as an emergent property of the system's hierarchical network architecture.

Reduced responsiveness of the chemotaxis system to perturbations in biochemical parameters. It is presented as a related system property arising from network architecture and contributing to stability.
Changes in biochemical parameters that challenge the chemotaxis system. The text uses these perturbations to describe the system's robustness and insensitivity to internal variation.
The layered organizational structure of the chemotaxis signaling network. It is described as the basis for robustness and insensitivity to perturbations in biochemical parameters.
The diverse environmental inputs sensed by bacterial chemoreceptors. These stimuli are detected through receptors with different sensory modalities and drive the chemotaxis response.
The distinct sensing capabilities of chemoreceptors that allow recognition of different stimuli. They are important for enabling bacteria to respond to multiple environmental cues.

A bacterial subject/population used as the biological model for studying chemotaxis and memory effects. It is the organism whose movement and signaling behavior are being described in relation to receptor methylation and tumbling control.

The broader microbial population context for the chemotaxis phenomenon discussed in the paper. It represents the class of organisms in which slow methylation of chemoreceptors and nonlocal chemotactic response are considered.
The directed movement process of bacteria in response to chemical gradients. In this text, it is the central biological process being modeled, with emphasis on memory effects and nonlocal response.

A signaling/adaptation process in which bacterial chemoreceptors undergo slow methylation. It introduces intrinsic time and length scales that affect chemotactic dynamics and invalidate simpler Keller-Segel descriptions under rapidly changing signals.
Receptor molecules on bacteria that detect chemical signals and undergo methylation. They are the molecular features whose slow modification underlies memory effects in chemotaxis.

A protein-level molecular feature that regulates bacterial tumbling behavior. The abstract states that its concentration field is used in the macroscopic description of chemotaxis, indicating a key role in movement control.

The spatial distribution or concentration of bacteria used as a macroscopic field in the kinetic description. It is coupled with the tumbling-control protein concentration to describe chemotactic behavior.

entity_name: CONCENTRATION FIELD OF THE PROTEIN THAT CONTROLS TUMBLING
description: A macroscopic field variable representing the concentration of the tumbling-control protein. It is part of the derived equations used to model chemotaxis and nonlocal response.
Derived continuum-level equations describing the coupled fields governing bacterial chemotaxis. They provide the analytical framework for capturing nonlocal response and memory effects.

A classical chemotaxis modeling framework that is stated to become invalid when chemical signals vary on the intrinsic time and length scales introduced by receptor methylation. It serves as the comparator model in the paper.

The environmental chemical gradient or signaling input that drives bacterial chemotaxis. In this context, its temporal and spatial variation determines whether standard Keller-Segel equations remain valid.

The environmental contexts in which chemical signals may change on the relevant time and length scales. These settings motivate the need for a model that accounts for memory effects and nonlocal response.

A response pattern in which bacterial chemotactic behavior depends on spatially or temporally extended information rather than purely local conditions. It is the key emergent behavior described by the derived macroscopic equations.

The bacterial organism discussed as the model system for studying chemotaxis. It serves as the subject in which the pathway architecture, signal transduction, adaptation, and swimming behavior are analyzed.

The sensory signaling process in Escherichia coli that mediates detection of environmental changes and directs bacterial movement. It is described as a highly conserved pathway composed of signal transduction and adaptation modules.

A functional module within the chemotaxis pathway that detects and amplifies environmental changes and rapidly transmits signals to control swimming behavior. It is the first module whose activity is modulated by adaptation.

A functional module within the chemotaxis pathway that gradually resets the activity and sensitivity of the signal transduction module after stimulation. It enables temporal comparison during chemotaxis.
The process by which environmental signals are detected, amplified, and transmitted within the chemotaxis pathway. It is central to converting external conditions into behavioral output.
The process that restores pathway responsiveness after initial stimulation by resetting activity and sensitivity. It supports temporal comparisons and sustained chemotactic performance.
The external conditions sensed by the chemotaxis pathway. Changes in this setting are detected and amplified by the signal transduction module.
The behavioral output controlled by the chemotaxis pathway. It reflects the downstream functional consequence of signal transduction and adaptation in response to environmental cues.
The comparison of environmental conditions over time enabled by adaptation in the chemotaxis pathway. This process is necessary for effective bacterial chemotaxis.

Quantitative features arising from the interplay between the chemotaxis pathway modules, as highlighted by experimental and theoretical work. In this context, it represents an emergent analytical concept used to rationalize pathway behavior.
The conceptual framework used to rationalize the emergent properties of chemotactic behavior. It links pathway architecture and function to evolutionary adaptation.
